original_value: We focus on the problem of training a deep neural network in generations. The flowchart is that, in order to optimize the target network (student), another network (teacher) with the same architecture is first trained, and used to provide part of supervision signals in the next stage. While this strategy leads to a higher accuracy, many aspects (e.g., why teacher-student optimization helps) still need further explorations.This paper studies this problem from a perspective of controlling the strictness in training the teacher network. Existing approaches mostly used a hard distribution (e.g., one-hot vectors) in training, leading to a strict teacher which itself has a high accuracy, but we argue that the teacher needs to be more tolerant, although this often implies a lower accuracy. The implementation is very easy, with merely an extra loss term added to the teacher network, facilitating a few secondary classes to emerge and complement to the primary class. Consequently, the teacher provides a milder supervision signal (a less peaked distribution), and makes it possible for the student to learn from inter-class similarity and potentially lower the risk of over-fitting. Experiments are performed on standard image classification tasks (CIFAR100 and ILSVRC2012). Although the teacher network behaves less powerful, the students show a persistent ability growth and eventually achieve higher classification accuracies than other competitors. Model ensemble and transfer feature extraction also verify the effectiveness of our approach.

result.paraphrase: We address the problem of training deep neural networks in generations. In this scheme, to optimize the target network (student), another network with the same architecture (teacher) is trained first and then used to supply part of the supervision in the next stage. Although this approach improves accuracy, many questions, such as why teacher-student optimization works, still require further study. This paper examines the issue by controlling how strict the teacher network is during training. Most existing methods use a hard target distribution, such as one-hot vectors, which produces a strict teacher with high accuracy; however, we argue that the teacher should be more tolerant, even if that often means lower accuracy. The method is simple: add only one extra loss term to the teacher network, allowing several secondary classes to appear and complement the primary class. As a result, the teacher gives a softer supervision signal with a less peaked distribution, enabling the student to learn inter-class similarity and potentially reducing overfitting. We evaluate the approach on standard image classification benchmarks, CIFAR100 and ILSVRC2012. Even though the teacher is less powerful, the students keep improving and ultimately achieve higher classification accuracy than competing methods. Model ensembling and transfer feature extraction further confirm the effectiveness of our approach.
